problem: VLM-based grounding and scene-graph EQA/navigation systems commit to a single action or target and are weak at metric-semantic queries such as 'two meters to the right of the fridge'. They tend to pick the nearest object satisfying a predicate without enforcing the metric offset or a consistent frame of reference.
motivation: Humans mix metric and semantic specifications in instructions, and a robot needs a planner-ready continuous goal in a metric 3D frame. VLMs have unstable distance estimates and frame-of-reference ambiguity, and scene graphs lack metric goal information. The paper therefore has VLMs supply only semantic and kernel parameters, and composes them analytically.
key_idea: Decompose a metric-semantic query into anchor, predicate and metric parts, use VLM agents to ground the anchor and set the parameters of analytic kernels (von Mises-Fisher and radial Gaussian), and multiply the kernels into a goal density over 3D free space from which a planner samples waypoints.
insight: The gains come from the pipeline structure (decomposition plus analytic composition) rather than from prompting. Replacing the explicit spatial reasoner with a single chain-of-thought planner drops object-selection SR from 0.42 to 0.20, and under occlusion the explicit reasoner gives 0.50 versus 0.30. Results vary across VLM backbones, so the structure fixes metric error while the backbone sets the trade-off. Failures mostly come from incomplete scene graphs, frame-of-reference ambiguity and map misalignment.
method: Orchestrator: parses the query into Spatial Description Clauses (anchor object, spatial predicate, metric constraint) using dependency parsing and templates; multiple clauses form conjunctions.

Grounding Agent: resolves the anchor against the online 3D scene graph using string similarity, CLIP crop-text similarity and a spatial salience prior, and maintains a belief B_t over referents in a shared memory ledger.

Spatial Agent: builds a PDF from a von Mises-Fisher directional kernel in the object-local frame (rotated by R_o about anchor t_o) and a radial Gaussian metric kernel, with parameters (theta0, phi0, kappa, d0, sigma_m) set by the VLM.

Cascading kernels: for compound queries, the per-anchor kernels are warped to global coordinates, added in log space (approximating a product of experts) and normalized into a possibly multimodal density.
Verifier: checks coherence of the grounding and triggers corrective retries.
Planner interface: takes the top-k samples or the peak of P(x) and passes them as waypoints to an RRT* planner, with new observations updating the scene graph in a closed loop.
MAPG-Bench: a human-annotated benchmark of 30 HM3D scenes and 100 metric-semantic queries in Habitat-Sim, with ground truth as 3D allocentric points.

numbers_note: MAPG-Bench split is not named in the paper (the benchmark is evaluation-only), so 'test' is used. The HM-EQA split is not stated, so 'val' is used. The Table 1 column values for Gemini 3 Pro (dErr_OO 0.58, dErr_OW 0.08, TSR 0.46) are omitted. The MAPG-Bench text and table contradict each other on which variant reaches the best O-O and O-W errors. The real-world demo is qualitative only (3 queries).
results: On MAPG-Bench, MAPG (GPT-5.2) cuts object-to-world error from GraphEQA's 5.82 m to 0.07 m, yaw from 13.5° to 1.9°, pitch from 27.9° to 4.4°, and raises TSR from 0.78 to 0.98. On HM-EQA, MAPG (Claude Opus 4.6) reaches 0.71 accuracy versus 0.67 for GraphEQA (Gemini 2.5 Pro).
limitations: Performance depends on scene-graph completeness: occluded objects never enter the map, and map/scene-graph misalignment blurs the belief map.
Frame-of-reference ambiguity (front/behind) and commonsense queries remain weak (commonsense accuracy 0.08-0.30).
The benchmark is small (100 queries, 30 scenes), the real-world demo has only 3 queries and an offline scene graph, and the kernel families are hand-chosen and domain-specific.
builds_on: Product of experts / compositional generative modeling
